sources.text:
With just days remaining before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the Trump administration continues to take losses in court over voting rolls. This latest one comes in California.
A 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals panel ruled 2-1 Friday against the Justice Department’s request to temporarily block California from counting 20,000 ballots. The administration claimed those ballots were from noncitizens.
Download the Straight Arrow app today to get the stories that matter free from manipulation, bias or agenda.
Point phone camera here
It’s the second time in less than a week that the appeals court has rejected the administration’s efforts.
This began on Oct. 15 when the DOJ sued the Golden State, alleging that more than 20,000 people who were likely noncitizens had been registered to vote and received mail-in ballots. Voting by noncitizens in federal elections is illegal.
The feds said they identified the individuals by comparing publicly available voter registration records with federal immigration data.
However, California officials have challenged the reliability of the federal government’s list, arguing that it could include eligible American citizens.
The administration wanted California election officials to separate the disputed ballots and verify the citizenship of those who cast them before counting their votes.
The appeals court rejected that request, agreeing with a lower court’s concerns that there was no practical way to identify and separate the ballots without potentially disrupting the election process and disenfranchising eligible voters.
“As the district court found — and we discern no clear error — there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system,” the appeals court wrote.
The court also emphasized that the Constitution gives states primary authority over administering elections.
Federal election laws also limit major changes to voter registration procedures within 90 days of an election.
The court argued that if the federal government wants different procedures for handling mail-in ballots, it should take that proposal to Congress rather than trying to impose the changes through litigation.
Only Judge Patrick Bumatay, a Trump appointee, ruled in favor of the federal government. He argued the administration’s proposal was a reasonable way to protect election integrity.
The administration has lost more than two dozen of these kinds of cases in federal court.
Despite that, President Trump has also continued making claims about election integrity in California, including recently suggesting that he would have won the state in previous elections if its vote counts had been honest. He has provided no evidence supporting those claims.
The Trump administration could appeal the 9th Circuit’s decision to the U.S. Supreme Court.

sources.text:
Trump loses appeals over California ballots, Homeland Security operations
Election workers sort ballots at an election operations facility in Martinez, California, on May 27, 2026, ahead of California’s statewide primary election. (Photo by Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images)
A federal appeals court on Friday denied a Trump administration demand that California set aside and not count the ballots of 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters, setting the stage for a possible appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.
A three-judge panel of the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against a U.S. Department of Justice request for an emergency order that would have required state and local election officials to not tabulate the ballots of voters on a list developed by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security unless they could prove their citizenship.
A separate 9th Circuit panel on Friday also denied a Justice Department request to allow Homeland Security to restart election-related field operations that could sweep up U.S. citizens. Civil rights groups had warned the operations put naturalized citizens at risk of disenfranchisement.
The rulings marked the third and fourth courtroom losses in less than a week for President Donald Trump’s administration in its 11th-hour legal campaign to assert authority over elections, which under the U.S. Constitution are administered by states.
“Exercising the power endowed to it by the Constitution, California comprehensively administers its elections, including by regulating voter eligibility,” the panel wrote in an unsigned majority opinion over California’s ballot counting.
The Justice Department in October provided California election officials with a list of approximately 20,000 individuals that it said were likely noncitizens registered to vote in the state. The DOJ cited a federal misdemeanor crime against noncitizen voting in demanding their ballots be set aside.
The DOJ says Homeland Security compiled the list after obtaining a public copy of California’s voter roll and checking it against government records and information from the LexisNexis research service. Officials in California and Los Angeles County have questioned the list’s accuracy and warned against relying on it to prevent the tabulation of ballots.
The Trump administration has gone to extraordinary lengths to pressure California election officials to set aside the ballots.
It sued just 48 hours after giving election officials the list of 20,000 voters and since then, DOJ lawyers have raised the possibility that state and local officials could face criminal prosecution if they count the ballots of noncitizens. Grand jury subpoenas have been sent to election officials in Los Angeles County.
Risks ‘uncertain,’ panel says
The appeals court’s decision in the California ballots case upheld a ruling from Judge David Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, against the Justice Department. In a blistering decision, Carter wrote that the Trump administration was attempting to coerce California that evidence existed of federal interference.
Carter also echoed concerns raised by election officials over the origin of the list. The 9th Circuit panel voiced similar worries in its Friday decision and said the Justice Department request risks disenfranchising voters.
“There is a public interest in maintaining the integrity of elections,” the opinion says. “But as discussed, the district court found that the risks that noncitizens are voting are, at best, uncertain, and also tempered by California’s established voter-eligibility procedures.”
The 9th Circuit also previously rejected a preemptive appeal filed by the Justice Department.
Appellate Judge Patrick Bumatay, a Trump appointee, wrote in a dissent that he would have granted the Justice Department’s request. He wrote that the DOJ was seeking “limited relief” and that the federal government and the states can work together.
“California decided long ago that aliens can’t vote in its elections. Today, the federal government merely seeks to safeguard that decision. We should have let them try,” Bumatay wrote.
The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment and a question about whether it would appeal.
“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in an earlier statement.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said in a social media post that the Trump administration’s three court losses over the past week make clear it has “zero authority to interfere in California’s elections.”
DHS election-related operations blocked
Another 9th Circuit panel on Friday affirmed a district court judge’s decision prohibiting DHS from conducting operations that could sweep up U.S. citizens. The prohibition applies in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin until polls close on Election Day.
A Homeland Security Investigations internal memo dated Aug. 31 describes a “surge initiative” beginning Sept. 1 that includes conducting field interviews. The memo, which was filed in court, identifies those states as targets of the surge during September. Additional locations are redacted in the document.
In an unsigned opinion, the panel questioned the Trump administration’s timing in pursuing a surge in voter fraud enforcement just before Election Day. The federal law enforcement activity is ostensibly focused on past voter fraud, the judges wrote, meaning that DHS had more than a year to pursue investigations before the pre-election period.
“The Federal Defendants have not indicated why restrictions on the Surge now prevent them from conducting these operations,” the panel wrote. “Nor have they explained why an injunction enjoining specific aspects of the Surge through Election Day causes irreparable harm when implementation of the Initiative can resume on November 4, 2026” — the day after Election Day.
The original lawsuit was filed by San Francisco, Santa Clara, the California Nurses Association, National Nurses United and the Voto Latino Foundation. They alleged voters, especially naturalized citizens, are at risk of intimidation and fear they could be wrongly targeted, the groups warned.
“Last week, the district court held that DHS’s frantic, last-minute voter investigations are unlawful voter intimidation. Today, the government’s attempt to restart that campaign failed,” Beau Tremitiere, a lawyer at Protect Democracy, said in a statement.
“This was one more desperate attempt by the Trump administration to interfere in the midterm elections, and the courts have again said no.”
Supreme Court next?
How the Supreme Court would rule if the Justice Department appeals either of these cases is unknown.
Conservatives hold six of its nine seats. The majority upended the electoral landscape earlier this year when it sharply weakened federal protections against racial gerrymandering, paving the way for Southern states to quickly redraw their congressional maps to favor Republicans.
But the Supreme Court has generally held that federal courts shouldn’t order dramatic changes just ahead of elections. For example, in September the justices repeatedly rejected requests to overturn a Missouri Supreme Court decision blocking a GOP gerrymander.
In the California ballots case, the 9th Circuit panel majority — which included Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, and Judge Gabriel Sanchez, an appointee of President Joe Biden — invoked that principle in denying the Trump administration’s request.
“Major concerns remain that granting the United States’s requested relief might … harm the public interest by risking the disenfranchisement of eligible voters and putting the entire tabulation process in jeopardy,” they wrote.

sources.news_title: JUST IN: Ninth Circuit Turns Down Trump DOJ’s Eleventh-Hour Push to Set Aside 20,000 California Ballots Tied to Suspected Non-Citizens – 100PercentFedUp.com – by Jack
sources.text:
The Trump Justice Department just took another emergency swing at California’s ballot-counting rules—and a divided Ninth Circuit panel knocked it down.
In a 2-1 ruling Friday, the appeals court refused to force California to segregate mail ballots connected to more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government believes are likely noncitizens.
That means California can keep processing those ballots under its existing election procedures with Election Day only days away.
But the decision was anything but unanimous.
Judge Patrick Bumatay, a Trump appointee, issued a blistering dissent warning that potentially unlawful votes could be mixed with legitimate ballots before officials determine whether the people who cast them are eligible.
And now the fight appears headed straight toward the Supreme Court.
The dispute began after federal investigators compared California voter-registration records with immigration and identity databases.
The Justice Department said that analysis identified more than 20,000 people it believes are likely noncitizens who were registered to vote and mailed ballots for the federal election.
Federal officials gave California a list of the names and asked the state to review them, verify citizenship and set aside any returned ballots until each voter’s eligibility could be established.
The department said Homeland Security Investigations worked with federal partners to compare public voter-registration records against immigration and identity data. Officials described the results as a list of people they believed were likely noncitizens—not a final court judgment that every person on it was ineligible.
The timing became central to the fight. California mailed ballots to registered voters on October 1, while the federal government delivered its list on October 13 and demanded a response within 48 hours.
California refused.
The state disputed the reliability of the federal list and argued that the demand came too late to rewrite ballot-processing rules in the middle of an election.
The DOJ then sued California and Los Angeles County on October 15.
Its requested remedy was narrow but consequential: preserve the disputed ballots without tabulating them until officials could verify the voters’ citizenship.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli made that distinction explicit as the case raced through the courts.
@TheJusticeDept is committed to seeking a court order to separate the suspected 20,000 noncitizen ballots from lawful ballots. This is necessary because California is already processing hundreds of thousands of ballots that cannot be undone.
Segregating a ballot does not prevent it from being counted later. It is designed to preserve the status quo and prevent the infection of our election with illegal ballots. https://t.co/ttE4HWm1zj
— F.A. United States Attorney Bill Essayli (@USAttyEssayli) October 28, 2026
U.S. District Judge David Carter rejected the government’s request for a temporary restraining order Wednesday.
Carter said federal prosecutors have a remedy available when they can prove that a noncitizen voted: bring a criminal case under federal law.
He also warned the Justice Department to stop threatening state and county election officials.
UPDATE: Judge Carter ends his hearing with a warning to DOJ:
“This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately. Good night.”
He will issue a formal ruling tomorrow but appears to be rejecting DOJ’s emergency efforts.
— Kyle Cheney (@kyledcheney) October 27, 2026
The DOJ immediately appealed and asked the Ninth Circuit for emergency relief.
That brought the case back before the same three-judge panel that had already rejected an earlier attempt to leapfrog the district court before Carter ruled.
This time, the panel reached the government’s renewed request after the lower court’s written denial.
Judges Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, and Gabriel Sanchez, a Biden appointee, formed the majority.
The court’s order concluded that the Justice Department had not carried the heavy burden required for an injunction pending appeal. The decision therefore leaves the district court’s denial and California’s current procedures in place.
The majority said there were serious concerns that granting the government’s request could disenfranchise eligible voters and throw California’s tabulation process into jeopardy.
The judges also relied on the district court’s doubts about the reliability of the government’s list.
They concluded that the government had not shown it was likely to prevail on the legal theories behind its request. The majority said the federal criminal ban on noncitizen voting does not itself hand the executive branch a private civil cause of action to redesign a state’s ballot-challenge process.
The panel also said Congress had not used its Elections Clause power to replace California’s procedures with the emergency system the DOJ wanted the courts to impose.
Without that congressional command, the majority said California’s existing statutory process remains controlling.
That point matters because the DOJ’s case does not rest on a judicial finding that all 20,000 people are noncitizens.
It rests on federal agencies’ conclusion that they are likely noncitizens and should be checked before their ballots are mixed into the count.
California says the list contains major errors and could sweep in eligible citizens.
The DOJ says waiting until after potentially unlawful ballots are mixed with lawful ones makes the harm impossible to undo.
That is the central collision in the case.
California argues that changing the process now could unlawfully burden voters and disrupt an election already underway.
The federal government argues that refusing to separate disputed ballots risks diluting the votes of eligible American citizens.
Essayli laid out the government’s position in an interview after the district-court hearing.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli BACKSLAPS California for allowing noncitizens on their voter rolls: “The entire purpose of our lawsuit is to prevent illegal ballots from being cast and counted in the upcoming election. The United States not only has an interest in prosecuting people, but we have an interest in preventing those ballots from being co-mingled with lawful American voters.”
— RedWave Press (@RedWavePress) October 28, 2026
The majority also pointed to Congress’s 90-day quiet period for sweeping voter-roll changes before a federal election.
It said the reliability concerns surrounding the federal list reflected exactly the danger that rule is designed to reduce.
The judges further rejected the DOJ’s attempt to use a federal criminal law banning noncitizen voting as a vehicle for ordering California to adopt a new ballot-challenge procedure.
In the majority’s view, Congress has not exercised its Elections Clause authority to replace California’s established rules with the process the executive branch requested.
Bumatay saw the case very differently.
He argued that both federal and state law prohibit noncitizens from voting and that the government proposed a modest way to preserve the disputed ballots while officials checked eligibility.
Separating a ballot, he stressed, does not cancel it.
It simply prevents the ballot from being irreversibly mixed with the broader count before the voter’s eligibility is resolved.
Bumatay accused the district court and his two colleagues of refusing a reasonable election-integrity safeguard even though the government says the threat is immediate.
The Associated Press reported that Justice Department lawyers have already indicated they will appeal the Ninth Circuit’s decision.
That would put the dispute before the U.S. Supreme Court just days before the November 3 election.
The report also noted that the majority was made up of one Trump appointee and one Biden appointee, while the dissent came from another Trump appointee. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed, and California election officials say that once a verified ballot is separated from its identifying envelope and mixed with other ballots, it cannot be traced back to the voter who submitted it.
That logistical reality is why both sides describe the clock as decisive.
The DOJ says every additional processed ballot risks an irreversible dilution of lawful votes. California says a court-ordered segregation plan this late could wrongly burden eligible citizens and destabilize a statewide count already in motion.
The larger lawsuit is not over.
Nor has any court made a final determination about the citizenship of every person on the federal list.
But the immediate question has now been answered twice by the Ninth Circuit.
California will not be ordered to segregate the disputed ballots before the election—unless the Supreme Court steps in.
For the Trump DOJ, that makes the next move as obvious as it is urgent.

sources.text:
DOJ loses new appeal for order purging 20,000 ‘suspect’ ballots
LOS ANGELES (KESQ) - The Justice Department today lost its second bid to have an appeals court stop California election officials from processing more than 20,000 ballots from people the federal government suspects may be non-citizens but are registered to vote in next week's election.
The renewed effort was filed with the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals immediately after a Los Angeles federal judge late Wednesday denied the DOJ's attempt to obtain a temporary restraining order separating the allegedly ineligible vote-by-mail ballots.
The 2-1 vote Friday to reject the appeal is the latest setback for the Trump administration's efforts to assert control over state-run elections.
"Because Congress has not exercised the specific power granted to it under the Elections Clause to override California's established laws for challenging ballots or removing ineligible voters, the State Legislature's statutory scheme remains the only method to do so,'' the appellate panel found.
In a forceful opinion this week, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter said the federal government's request "would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.''
The judge set an expedited hearing for Nov. 13 in Los Angeles federal court to further explore the matter. Carter said election officials have until Dec. 3 -- the date by which election results must be certified -- to resolve the issue, suggesting there was no need for an emergency injunction.
Carter indicated he would call witnesses to determine the reliability of the methodology and data that prosecutors used in creating the list of 20,000 possible non-citizens. He said previously that federal officials provided only vague explanations ``and raised multiple questions regarding reliability'' of the process.
In asking for a quick ruling on the renewed motion, the DOJ wrote that "once a vote-by-mail ballot has been processed, it cannot be undone if it is later determined that the voter was ineligible."
Federal prosecutors filed their first application for an emergency order with the 9th Circuit last week, before Carter ruled on the matter. The three-judge appellate panel quickly rebuffed the effort following a rare Sunday hearing.
In his subsequent ruling, Carter wrote that by moving to have ballots sequestered, the Trump administration embarked on "a broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference.''
On Thursday, federal prosecutors pursued subpoenas of California state and local election officials in connection with alleged illegal voting in next week's midterm elections.
The action was seen as an expansion of the Trump administration's efforts to show that thousands of non-citizens are registered on California's voter rolls.
The DOJ issued a statement pointing out that receiving a subpoena "doesn't mean you are a target'' of criminal prosecution.
The federal government sued California on Oct. 15, more than a week after mail ballots were sent to all registered voters, demanding it set aside 20,000 ballots from alleged non-citizens after the state refused to voluntarily sequester those votes.
Carter, a Bill Clinton appointee who is overseeing the closely watched lawsuit, United States of America v. State of California, et al., previously dismissed a DOJ attempt to force California to turn over its full voter registration list to the federal government.
The Justice Department has sued 30 states that refused to turn over voter data, losing the majority of the cases so far.
In opposition to the administration's demand for an injunction, Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan argued they lack the mechanisms and legal authority to freeze mail ballots until voters' citizenship can be verified.
"Voting is already underway in Los Angeles County,'' the motion states. "Ballots have been mailed, returned and processed, and election officials are working toward fixed deadlines for counting and certification. Plaintiff United States of America, through the Department of Justice ... now asks this court to interrupt that work and enjoin the withholding of 20,000 registered California voters' ballots pending investigation based solely on an unreliable voter roll maintenance list."
The Trump administration has long alleged that large numbers of non-citizens were casting ballots in California and elsewhere, but officials have not provided proof or documentation of widespread fraud.
"Three legal victories in one week make clear that the Trump Administration has zero authority to interfere in California's elections,'' state Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement. "California law makes it illegal for non-citizens to vote in federal elections, and there are several state laws that guard against it. That is why it is exceptionally rare. The administration's baseless claims of widespread fraud are an attempt to sow doubt in our democratic process and risk disenfranchising eligible voters. We will keep fighting to uphold the rule of law."
Gov. Gavin Newsom also commended the appeals court ruling.
"Trump and his administration just lost for the third time this week in their desperate and dangerous attempts to meddle in the California election process with voting already underway and just days before Election Day,'' Newsom said. "These attacks on our democracy are serious, and the full force of our state is defending our democracy right now. We will continue to fight them on their illegal power grabs every step of the way, and deliver a free and fair election just as we've always done."

A federal appeals court on Friday denied the Justice Department’s emergency request to order California to set aside mail ballots from about 20,000 alleged “likely noncitizens,” finding the government hadn’t shown it was clearly entitled to the extraordinary relief days before the midterm election.

In a 2-1 ruling Friday, the appeals court refused to force California to segregate mail ballots connected to more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government believes are likely noncitizens.
That means California can keep processing those ballots under its existing election procedures with Election Day only days away.
But the decision was anything but unanimous.
Judge Patrick Bumatay, a Trump appointee, issued a blistering dissent warning that potentially unlawful votes could be mixed with legitimate ballots before officials determine whether the people who cast them are eligible.
And now the fight appears headed straight toward the Supreme Court.
The dispute began after federal investigators compared California voter-registration records with immigration and identity databases.
The Justice Department said that analysis identified more than 20,000 people it believes are likely noncitizens who were registered to vote and mailed ballots for the federal election.
Federal officials gave California a list of the names and asked the state to review them, verify citizenship and set aside any returned ballots until each voter’s eligibility could be established.
The department said Homeland Security Investigations worked with federal partners to compare public voter-registration records against immigration and identity data. Officials described the results as a list of people they believed were likely noncitizens—not a final court judgment that every person on it was ineligible.
The timing became central to the fight. California mailed ballots to registered voters on October 1, while the federal government delivered its list on October 13 and demanded a response within 48 hours.
California refused.
The state disputed the reliability of the federal list and argued that the demand came too late to rewrite ballot-processing rules in the middle of an election.
The DOJ then sued California and Los Angeles County on October 15.
Its requested remedy was narrow but consequential: preserve the disputed ballots without tabulating them until officials could verify the voters’ citizenship.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli made that distinction explicit as the case raced through the courts.
@TheJusticeDept is committed to seeking a court order to separate the suspected 20,000 noncitizen ballots from lawful ballots. This is necessary because California is already processing hundreds of thousands of ballots that cannot be undone.
Segregating a ballot does not prevent it from being counted later. It is designed to preserve the status quo and prevent the infection of our election with illegal ballots. https://t.co/ttE4HWm1zj
— F.A. United States Attorney Bill Essayli (@USAttyEssayli) October 28, 2026
U.S. District Judge David Carter rejected the government’s request for a temporary restraining order Wednesday.
Carter said federal prosecutors have a remedy available when they can prove that a noncitizen voted: bring a criminal case under federal law.
He also warned the Justice Department to stop threatening state and county election officials.
UPDATE: Judge Carter ends his hearing with a warning to DOJ:

He will issue a formal ruling tomorrow but appears to be rejecting DOJ’s emergency efforts.
— Kyle Cheney (@kyledcheney) October 27, 2026

California says the list contains major errors and could sweep in eligible citizens.

— RedWave Press (@RedWavePress) October 28, 2026
The majority also pointed to Congress’s 90-day quiet period for sweeping voter-roll changes before a federal election.
It said the reliability concerns surrounding the federal list reflected exactly the danger that rule is designed to reduce.
The judges further rejected the DOJ’s attempt to use a federal criminal law banning noncitizen voting as a vehicle for ordering California to adopt a new ballot-challenge procedure.
In the majority’s view, Congress has not exercised its Elections Clause authority to replace California’s established rules with the process the executive branch requested.

He argued that both federal and state law prohibit noncitizens from voting and that the government proposed a modest way to preserve the disputed ballots while officials checked eligibility.

Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed, and California election officials say that once a verified ballot is separated from its identifying envelope and mixed with other ballots, it cannot be traced back to the voter who submitted it.
That logistical reality is why both sides describe the clock as decisive.
The DOJ says every additional processed ballot risks an irreversible dilution of lawful votes. California says a court-ordered segregation plan this late could wrongly burden eligible citizens and destabilize a statewide count already in motion.
The larger lawsuit is not over.
Nor has any court made a final determination about the citizenship of every person on the federal list.
But the immediate question has now been answered twice by the Ninth Circuit.
California will not be ordered to segregate the disputed ballots before the election—unless the Supreme Court steps in.

9th Circuit again denies Trump administration request to block 20,000 California ballots
LOS ANGELES — A federal appeals court for the second time Friday denied a Trump administration request to block 20,000 ballots from California voters the administration believes may be noncitizens — ruling that the administration had failed to show that “such extraordinary relief, during an ongoing election, is clearly required by law.”
The three-judge panel of the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals — composed of two appointees of President Donald Trump and one of President Joe Biden — ruled that the U.S. Constitution gives the state and Congress the power to decide how elections are run, and that allowing the Trump administration to “misuse” federal statutes to “prescribe” how California must process ballots would “override the plain and manifest dictates of the Constitution itself.”
“Because Congress has not exercised the specific power granted to it under the Elections Clause to override California’s established laws for challenging ballots or removing ineligible voters, the State Legislature’s statutory scheme remains the only method to do so,” the judges found.
The judges wrote that “if the United States believes different procedures are necessary for vote-by-mail ballots, we believe it should take that suggestion to Congress, not the courts.”
They also wrote that separate federal law prescribes sweeping changes to voter lists 90 days prior to an election, especially given questions about the reliability of the Trump administration’s list of purported noncitizens.
“The suspect reliability of these lists found by the district court reflects the concern Congress sought to mitigate with the 90-day quiet period,” they wrote.
Judge Patrick J. Bumatay, the other Trump appointee on the panel, dissented — arguing that his colleagues erred in denying a basic request by the Trump administration to ensure only citizens are voting.
“The federal government proposes a modest remedy — stopping California from mixing the ballots of citizens and suspected noncitizens,” Bumatay wrote. “This solution would not cancel any vote but would allow time to verify the eligibility of suspected noncitizens. The district court, and now our court, denies this reasonable request.”

sources.news_title: Appeals court rejects DOJ's demand for California to set aside disputed ballots
sources.text:
The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday rejected the Justice Department’s request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election.
The panel’s 2-1 ruling is the latest setback for the Trump administration’s efforts to assert control over state-run elections.
The administration has alleged California sent ballots to some 20,000 people who may not be U.S. citizens. It wants the state to set those ballots aside and not count them until citizenship can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
A district court judge already forcefully denied that request and warned that the Justice Department’s demands could disenfranchise citizens.
“As the district court found — and we discern no clear error — there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system,” the appeals court wrote.
The ruling is the latest in an expansive legal battle between the federal government and the state before Election Day in the midterms Tuesday. Millions of people in California have already voted.
The majority opinion was authored by Judge Mark J. Bennett, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, and Judge Gabriel P. Sanchez, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden.
The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling.
Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. Elections officials have said that processed votes are completely anonymized and can’t be matched back to the voters who submitted them.
The ruling comes during broader federal scrutiny of local elections, with the Trump administration issuing a raft of subpoenas in Alaska in a spoiler-candidate controversy. The Justice Department has also provided a list of alleged noncitizen voters to officials in Washington state.
Outside groups sued for access to the disputed list
Earlier on Friday, a federal judge in Washington ordered the Trump administration to share the disputed list of names with lawyers for the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights and the UCLA Voting Rights Project. They want the list so they can examine who is on the list and assess its impact on eligible voters.
It will be the first time that a nongovernment organization will have the opportunity to evaluate the merits of the list of some 20,000 names.
Prosecutors with the Trump administration have argued that there is just as much to lose from noncitizens illegally voting, arguing that to tally those votes would dilute the voice of citizens.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra is an adviser to the UCLA Voting Rights Project.
The two groups sued the Homeland Security Department in early October to prevent it from using federal immigration data to challenge state voter rolls. The lawsuit cited examples in other states where the federal government’s data has been proven to mistakenly include thousands of citizens. It argued that the data-matching methods risk disenfranchising or deterring citizens from voting. On top of that, plaintiffs argued, the lists could disproportionately target naturalized citizens who are legally entitled to vote.
Another suit seeks to defend election workers
A coalition of unions on Friday also joined the growing list of groups challenging the federal government’s efforts.
The unions, including the A.F.L.-C.I.O. and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, are asking a federal judge to temporarily block the Justice Department from demanding that local officials stop counting ballots and to drop threats to criminally prosecute officials who do not comply with their demands.
The top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, Bill Essayli, has warned that “any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy.”
On Thursday the Associated Press obtained subpoenas issued to election officials in Los Angeles County. The subpoenas request any documents and communications related to letters sent in July and October by federal officials to state election officials outlining the allegations about noncitizen voters. They also seek any information about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted. At least three L.A. County election officials have been asked to appear before a grand jury on Nov. 4, the day after the election.
The lawsuit accuses the Justice Department of issuing threats against election officials that could interfere with their ability to process votes.
It is unclear whether the Justice Department intends to bring criminal charges against anyone. The department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.
